title: BMZ Poland and EVE develop LMFP battery for heavy-duty commercial vehicles - electrive.com
content:
BMZ Poland and Chinese cell manufacturer EVE Energy are jointly developing an LMFP battery for electric commercial vehicles. The Versora LMFP, presented at IAA Transportation, is said to offer advantages over LFP, including reduced weight, higher charging power, and better cold-weather performance. Series production is planned for mid-2028.
BMZ Poland is headquartered in Gliwice.
Image: BMZ
BMZ Poland and EVE Energy have agreed on a long-term strategic partnership. As their first joint project, the partners are expanding BMZ’s modular Versora battery platform to include lithium manganese iron phosphate cells (LMFP) from EVE. The focus is not only on electric trucks and buses but also on construction and agricultural machinery, special vehicles, and ships.
With LMFP, the companies position the new variant between the established cell chemistries LFP and NMC. LFP is known primarily for its low cost, safety, and longevity but has a lower energy density. NMC, on the other hand, offers higher energy density and strong performance across a wider temperature range but is more expensive.
For heavy-duty commercial vehicles, BMZ and EVE see LMFP as offering significant advantages in weight and charging speed. According to the companies, a corresponding battery system in an electric long-haul truck can be up to ten per cent lighter than a comparable LFP solution while meeting the same energy requirements. It should also support charging power of up to one megawatt or charging rates of 2.2C. This would allow the battery to charge from ten to 80 per cent in less than 25 minutes. For a comparable LFP solution, BMZ Poland cites around 35 minutes.
BMZ Poland also provides concrete figures for lifespan and cold-weather performance. The LMFP battery is expected to achieve more than 4,500 full charge cycles while maintaining 80 per cent State of Health. The next generation is targeted to exceed 5,500 cycles. At minus 20 degrees Celsius, 85 per cent of the capacity should remain available, compared to around 75 per cent for the LFP technology used by BMZ Poland for comparison.
Same platform for NMC and LMFP
Versora is designed as a modular battery platform. The Polish team uses two module formats that can be installed in the vehicle floor, body, or roof and combined according to energy and space requirements. This approach particularly targets manufacturers with different vehicle variants and body configurations.
A key advantage is the use of different cell chemistries within the same architecture. The NMC and LMFP versions are intended to have the same dimensions and weight, as well as identical electrical interfaces and voltage classes. Vehicle manufacturers could thus offer different battery variants without modifying the underlying vehicle architecture.
BMZ Poland is already active as a battery partner in the commercial vehicle sector. Among other projects, the company in Gliwice assembles the new
NMC4 battery generation for the Mercedes-Benz eCitaro
, which is set to be used in all variants of the electric bus from 2026. The Polish BMZ subsidiary was not affected by the insolvency of BMZ Germany GmbH and BMZ Holding GmbH at the end of 2025. Significant parts of the group were subsequently taken over by
, which had previously been involved as a minority shareholder. In the current company presentation, BMZ lists the investment company founded by Susanne Klatten as the owner of the group since 2025.
It will still be some time before the new LMFP version enters series production. The first customer samples are planned for 2027, with series deliveries set to begin in mid-2028. BMZ is further along with the NMC version of Versora: selected customers are already receiving the first samples, and series production is scheduled to start in 2027.

title: CATL unveils truck battery with up to 1,000 km range - electrive.com
content:
CATL has unveiled its Tectrans II battery solution for heavy-duty electric commercial vehicles at IAA Transportation. At its maximum capacity, it's said to offer a range of up to 1,000 km and, according to CATL, can be charged to 80 per cent in 25 minutes using megawatt-level fast charging.
Image: CATL
This week, CATL has pushed for the spotlight at IAA Transportation in Hannover by unveiling a new battery solution for commercial vehicles. In addition to heavy-duty trucks, Tectrans II is also suitable for medium-duty trucks and buses. The battery will therefore be available in various housing formats, as well as for installation in the underbody or on the roof. However, CATL’s new solution primarily targets long-haul electric transport, as the company’s representatives emphasised the peak values for range, charging time, and operating costs in long-distance applications during the presentation.
In its full configuration, the system promises ranges of up to 1,000 km (with no test cycle specified yet) and can be charged to 80 per cent in 25 minutes using megawatt fast charging. At the same time, the battery packs are designed to be adaptable so that they can be combined with both central vehicle drives and e-axles. Additionally, Tectrans II can theoretically be installed as a swappable battery. This is because CATL is also active in the battery-swapping business in China and plans a
corresponding effort in Europe in cooperation with Octopus Energy
According to CATL: thanks to the standardisation of the battery modules used, electrical interfaces, and communication protocols, both current and future vehicle models will be able to adopt future battery upgrades without major changes to their platforms. Given the dynamic development of battery technology, this is an important detail. Truck manufacturers will thus potentially need to make few adjustments to their vehicle platforms when adopting battery innovations.
As for the battery itself: It features a gravimetric energy density of 170 Wh/kg, which CATL states is approximately 13 per cent above the industry average. With the same battery capacity, vehicles can “carry about 0.6 tonnes of additional payload” as a result, according to the official presentation. The battery is also designed for a service life of 12 years and 1.5 million kilometres with 70 per cent capacity retention. New features include a newly developed, robust corrosion protection system and an even more stable base plate. CATL has not disclosed the cell chemistry, but it is likely that the system works with both LFP and NMC chemistries, as the Chinese manufacturer is proficient in both technology strands.
Die CATL Tectrans II-Batterie setzt auf standardisierte Module für die Zellen.
At the trade fair, CATL also signed a letter of intent with the DHL Group to develop green freight corridors in Europe. Building on a first agreement between the two parties from September 2024, CATL will, among other things, provide energy storage systems and energy management platforms for DHL’s logistics parks. There is also talk of establishing battery-swapping systems and ultra-fast charging systems, as well as pilot projects for future electric vehicles.
Zhu Lingbo, CTO of the CATL Global Business Unit, commented: “Commercial vehicle electrification will unfold over more than a decade. With our deep technological expertise and long-term commitment, CATL is ready to be the most reliable partner for customers worldwide and for the global electrification of freight transport.”
(DHL Group)

title: Growing Role of LFP Batteries in Global Energy Transition
content:
Lithium-Ion Batteries
Battery Applications
Industry Trends
Learn how LFP batteries are transforming commercial vehicles, marine energy storage, material testing, and supply chains worldwide.
September 16, 2026
4 Min Read
LANXESS develops iron oxides and iron phosphate as raw materials for cathode materials in LFP batteries.
Courtesy of LANXESS.
Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries are known for their high thermal stability, long cycle life, and affordability compared to nickel-based chemistries.
LFP batteries
are increasingly being adopted in sectors such as transportation, marine energy storage, and stationary applications. According to LANXESS, three-quarters of all electric vehicles (EVs) in China already use this battery chemistry. In Europe, management consultancy
Roland Berger
forecasts an LFP market share of 50% by 2030, up from 10% today.
The following recent announcements highlight the growing versatility of LFP technology, showcasing advancements in commercial vehicle applications, material testing, marine energy storage solutions, and the battery material supply chain.
Commercial vehicle applications: Buses and trucks
Cummins Inc. and its subsidiary Accelera
announced
plans to expand battery manufacturing in Europe to meet the growing demand for battery-electric solutions in the commercial vehicle market. The new facility in Spain will produce the Advanced LFP battery platform, specifically designed for demanding applications such as buses and trucks.
Related:
Q&A: Standardized Imaging Framework Enhances Battery Research Reliability
Amy Davis, president of Accelera and Components, emphasized the importance of local production: “Manufacturing in Spain strengthens our ability to support customers locally, while positioning us for long-term growth in the region.” This investment reflects Cummins’ commitment to providing scalable, reliable solutions for the European market, where the adoption of battery-electric commercial vehicles is accelerating. The Spain facility is expected to play a pivotal role in supporting the region’s transition to zero-emission transportation.
Electric truck at a container terminal. Courtesy of PhonlamaiPhoto/iStock / Getty Images Plus.
Testing the material properties of battery cells
Specialty chemicals company
has opened a new battery laboratory at its Krefeld-Uerdingen site in Germany. The laboratory focuses on testing and developing battery materials based on iron oxide and iron phosphate, critical components of LFP cathode materials.
Murat Gürsoy, Head of Innovation for Iron Oxides and Iron Phosphate at LANXESS, explained the laboratory’s role: “Today, cell manufacturers consider more than just raw material availability. What matters is the reliability of processing and its contribution to cell performance. This is precisely where our laboratory comes in. We bring material development and cell testing closer together. This gives us an earlier indication of whether a material works in a real cell assembly.”
In its battery laboratory, LANXESS tests the impact of different grades of iron oxide and iron phosphate in LFP materials directly within battery cells. Courtesy of Lanxess.
The facility can test the impact of different grades of iron oxide and iron phosphate directly within battery cells, accelerating the development of next-generation LFP batteries. This approach improves material reliability and, as a result, reduces dependence on Asian suppliers.
Related:
Donut Lab Battery Breakdown Highlights Importance of Independent Testing
Marine energy storage solutions
Corvus Energy AS, recently
unveiled
the Blue Whale NxtGen Power system, a high-power LFP energy storage solution developed in collaboration with BYD Energy Storage. The Blue Whale NxtGen Power system is tailored for vessels where power demand, rather than energy capacity, defines system performance. It is ideal for tugs, workboats, offshore vessels, and large ferries requiring rapid charging between crossings.
Thor Humerfelt, Head of Product Innovation at Corvus Energy, highlighted the advantages of the partnership: “LFP technology has advanced significantly in recent years and now offers a highly cost-effective solution for a wide range of maritime applications. By combining BYD Energy Storage’s technology leadership, manufacturing expertise, and global scale with Corvus Energy’s maritime experience, we can accelerate innovation, reduce system costs, and deliver even greater value to our customers.”
Blue Whale NxtGen Energy -the first LFP battery based on the NxtGen architecture. Courtesy of Corvus.
Battery material supply chain
The battery materials supply chain is undergoing significant transformation, as evidenced by the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) signed between E3 Lithium and Epsilon CAM. Epsilon CAM is a developer and manufacturer of LFP-based Cathode Active Materials (CAM) for lithium-ion batteries. The
agreement
contemplates the potential supply of maximum up to 5,000 tons per year of battery-grade lithium carbonate over a five-year term from E3’s Clearwater Project.
Related:
How Europe Can Lead the Solid-State Battery Race
Chris Doornbos, CEO & Chair of E3 Lithium, emphasized the importance of securing reliable supply chains: “Securing long-term offtake contracts is a critical commercial milestone required to advance the Clearwater Project. This MOU with Epsilon demonstrates a serious interest and draws a clear path from Alberta brine directly into the battery supply chain.” This collaboration highlights the growing need for diversified supply chains to support the rapid expansion of electric mobility and energy storage solutions.
The adoption of LFP batteries continues to gain momentum across industries, driven by their cost-effectiveness, safety, and versatility. Recent developments in commercial vehicle applications, material testing, marine energy storage solutions, and the battery material supply chain show that LFP batteries play a central role in the global transition to sustainable energy solutions.

title: Could AI Help In-Flight Drone Recharging Take Off?
content:
Charging
Automotive & Mobility
SunCubes is using SimScale’s Simulation Cloud and Physics AI tools to develop laser-based charging solutions for recharging drones and other autonomous systems in flight.
September 15, 2026
3 Min Read
SunCubes is designing wireless energy transfer hardware for recharging unmanned autonomous vehicles.
SunCubes
have to land and plug in to recharge their batteries? The team at
SunCubes
may have another solution.
The company is developing laser-based charging solutions that would let drones and other unmanned autonomous vehicles (UAVs) recharge in flight, or at remote stations, without physical contact, according to a news release. To give their vision wings, so to speak, SunCubes is using AI engineering tools from
SimScale
to support the design and validation of its UAV systems and wireless energy transfer hardware.
"SunCubes represents a genuinely new frontier for engineering simulation,” explained David Heiny, co-founder and CEO of SimScale, in the release. “Laser-based wireless charging for drones is one of the most technically demanding hardware challenges in the industry today, and seeing a team this focused on using AI-assisted simulation as a core design tool is exactly the future we're building toward."
Related:
BYD Expands Globally with Innovations in Battery Technology
The SunCubes team is using SimScale’s Simulation Cloud and Physics AI tools. “The combination allows us to cover different simulation domains while increasingly using AI to support all engineers with simulation setup, execution, and analysis,” Davide Russo, co-founder and chief innovation officer for SunCubes, tells
Design News
. “As we move closer to market, we are using SimScale primarily for the optimization and engineering validation of our products.”
SimScale’s tools complement those already used by the SunCubes team. “SimScale integrates well with the engineering tools we already use in our design workflow, including KiCad for PCB design and Onshape for mechanical design,” Russo says. “The integration with Onshape is particularly useful, as SimScale can access our CAD documents and projects directly. This removes the need to manually export models and upload them again whenever we want to run or update a simulation, making the iteration between design and simulation significantly faster.”
The SunCubes team is using AI to help with design, simulation, and validation. SUNCUBES
When asked whether Russo has any advice for other engineers on implementing and using AI, he says his team “sees particular value in AI when engineering involves repetitive or iterative simulation workflows.
“One example is multidisciplinary optimization, where the output of one analysis becomes an input or constraint for another. In the optimization of a drone architecture, for instance, structural optimization can affect thermal behavior, while the resulting thermal conditions can in turn change structural performance. This creates an iterative loop across multiple simulation domains. AI can help automate and manage these repeated analysis cycles rather than requiring engineers to manually rebuild and execute each iteration,” he says.
Related:
Schneider Electric Launches Home EV Charger That Works With Existing Electrical Systems
“Another strong use case is product families where geometry, dimensions or materials change between variants, but the underlying simulation methodology and setup remain largely the same. In these cases, AI agents can reproduce consistent simulation workflows across multiple designs, adapting the relevant parameters while maintaining the same analysis approach. This can significantly reduce repetitive engineering work as well as the computational effort associated with inefficient trial-and-error simulation,” Russo concludes.

title: Volvo XC60 PHEV Boasts 78-Mile Electric Range
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Design & Manufacturing
The Swedish automaker's upgraded plug-in hybrid crossover features a battery more than twice the size of its predecessor's power pack.
September 15, 2026
1 Min Read
2028 Volvo XC60.
Volvo Cars
At a Glance
The 2028 XC60 T8's 37.9-kWh usable battery capacity dwarfs the 18.8-kWh pack in the current model.
Combined system output reaches 455 hp when the turbocharged 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine activates.
Maximum non-stop range hits 590 miles when drivers utilize both full battery charge and gasoline tank.
The car industry continues to see
longer-range plug-in hybrids
as the bridge that will carry US drivers over the hump to eventually embrace
battery EVs
, and the 2028 Volvo XC60 T8 AWD Long-Range Plug-In Hybrid is the latest and most extreme example of this strategy.
The new XC60 PHEV will carry a 41.2-kilowatt-hour battery pack that has a usable capacity of 37.9 kWh. That compares to 18.8 kWh for the current model’s battery pack and to 24 kW for the original 2011
Nissan Leaf
battery-electric vehicle.
This provides a predicted electric-only driving range of 78 miles. Volvo notes that the media US Volvo driver commutes 22 miles round-trip daily, according to Strategic Vision, so they would be able to plug in the evening of the third day.
During EV driving, the electric drivetrain produces as much as 208 horsepower. When the turbocharged 2.0-liter I-4 engine engages, total system power equals 455 hp, which will push the XC60 T8 to 60 mph in 4.5 seconds.
Volvo doesn’t specify the power level of the onboard AC charger, but the company does say that the car’s battery pack can be charged to 100% in 5.7 hours on a Level 2 AC charger. Maximum driving range isn’t generally a relevant statistic for combustion vehicles, but when drivers use all of the battery capacity and all of the gas, the XC60 can go 590 miles non-stop.
The company will assemble the XC60 at its Torslanda, Sweden, and Charleston, South Carolina plants. As a 2028 model, Volvo has not announced when the new models will first reach customers.

title: How Tobias Meyer is Leading DHL's Sustainable Supply Chain

How Tobias Meyer is Leading DHL's Sustainable Supply Chain

Tobias Meyer, Chief Executive Officer of DHL Group, has been ranked second in Supply Chain Digital's Top 250 Supply Chain Leaders list (Credit: DHL Group)
Through his work towards Strategy 2030 and zero-emission mobility, Tobias Meyer, CEO of DHL Group, sits among the world’s top supply chain leaders
Tobias Meyer, Chief Executive Officer of DHL Group, has been ranked second in Supply Chain Digital's
Top 250 Supply Chain Leaders
He has spent more than a decade at DHL, covering a variety of roles before earning the CEO position in May 2023.
In his role, Tobias oversees an organisation operating across more than 220 countries and territories.
He constructed DHL’s Strategy 2030 after completing Strategy 2025 which sustainably lifted the company’s profitability across the transition.

Tobias Meyer, Chief Executive Officer of DHL. Credit: DHL Group / ANDREAS KUEHLKEN
Building a career across DHL's businesses
Tobias holds a doctorate in mechanical engineering from Technische Universität Darmstadt, having also studied Industrial Engineering at the University of Illinois.
He spent more than 12 years at
McKinsey & Company
across Frankfurt and Singapore, becoming a Partner specialising exclusively in transportation and logistics.
In 2013, he joined DHL as Executive Vice President of Corporate Development, before becoming Chief Operating Officer of DHL Global Forwarding.
He then led a successful turnaround as CEO of Post & Parcel Germany, having previously served as its Head of Operations and IT.
Following his success, Tobias joined the DHL Board of Management in 2019, four years before taking the CEO role.
Delivering Strategy 2030
Tobias took over as CEO midway through Strategy 2025, going on to complete the plan before creating its successor.
Strategy 2030 targets growth across DHL's core businesses alongside wider company growth initiatives.
The company says its plan is built on an “ambition to achieve net-zero GHG emissions in line with defined targets and centred on growth”.
It prioritises
supply chain resilience
, digital transformation and operational excellence across DHL's global network.
Under Tobias, DHL has accelerated adoption of advanced analytics, automation and AI to
improve supply chain visibility
, delivery reliability and warehouse efficiency.
In March 2026, the Supervisory Board of Deutsche Post AG extended his contract until March 2031, four years earlier than its original expiry date.
We want to decarbonise the transport sector now and regulation should not hinder but support us.
Tobias Meyer, CEO of DHL Group
Advancing sustainable logistics
Tobias is leading the push to implement zero-emission mobility across DHL's global network.
He has pursued sustainable aviation fuel partnerships as part of the
group's wider decarbonisation strategy
, targeting one of logistics' hardest-to-abate emissions sources.
In 2025, DHL and Scania ran a 100 day test on its Extended Range Electric Vehicle.
The company says it covered nearly 22,000 kilometres, operating more than 90% of the time in electric mode.
Tobias revealed that the vehicle saved around 46.5 tonnes of CO₂ compared with a diesel truck during the first half of 2026.

title: Why ePost Global Won the Global Trade and Logistics Award

ePost Global won gold for the Global Trade and Logistics Award
Following a night of celebration, Supply Chain Digital takes a look at the hard work behind ePost Global's win at the Global Supply Chain Awards
Amid ongoing volatility and logistics complexity, leaders gathered from around the world for an evening of celebration.
Throughout the night, companies were celebrated for their hard work maintaining operations amid turbulent relationships and as they integrate technology into their operations.
The first supply chain award of the night went to ePost Global, gaining the

and Logistics Award.
The Global Trade and Logistics Award
Global Trade & Logistics

title: Building Tomorrow's Supply Chain: Siemens' Success Story
content:
Building Tomorrow's Supply Chain: Siemens' Success Story
Prioritise Us
on Google
Alexander Tschentscher, VP of Supply Chain Strategy at Siemens, led the opening keynote on Day Two
Alexander Tschentscher of Siemens took to the stage at Supply Chain LIVE to explore how success is driven by people behind the technology
In a world dominated by technological innovation and digital advancements, the people behind this integration can often be overlooked.
However, without the people, there is no technology to undertake this
transformation
This is exactly the topic that was discussed by Alexander Tschentscher, Head of Supply Chain Excellence & Head of Strategy - Supply Chain & Logistics at Siemens, in his keynote speech which kicked off Day Two of Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit.
Behind the technology
Technology has become a core part of the everyday supply chain, with AI being seen as a driver of efficiency and resilience. However, recent years have also demonstrated how the technology can also act as a disruptor, with a rising number of cyber attacks revealing vulnerabilities.
Amid an event full of
AI strategists
and technology specialists, Alexander asked us to peek behind the curtain and explore why this technology is so successful. In his keynote speech that kicked off Day Two, Alexander spoke of the people behind the technology.
The presentation,
Building Tomorrow's Supply Chain: How People-Powered Strategy Drives Siemens' Success
, explored how fostering a human-centric approach has proven to drive operational excellence across global networks.
"AI is a big topic, but I also want to touch on something which I personally believe is very important: people," Alexander says.
Alexander was also a speaker Procurement and Supply Chain LIVE, London in 2025
Reflecting on success
In today's world, every business is facing some form of complexity in their supply chain, whether they are tackling the digital
transformation
, dealing with an ageing workforce, or being impacted by the wider geopolitical disrupters. It can be easy to measure success by how well a company is seemingly meeting these challenges, but Alexander points to something else.
"Everyone in this room," he says. "We have one common ground and this is people. We all have teams. We all are individuals and we all try to do the best we can every single day.
"My understanding is that performance is not driven by processes or technologies. It's driven by people. And they are the differentiator, the decisive factor for sustainable success."
Rather than taking to the stage and explaining solutions that have
worked for Siemens
, Alexander wanted to spark a thought. His presentation delved into reflection, looking at three core topics; perseverance, robust versus resilience and strategic thinking.
Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit 2026 took place alongside Procurement, Sustainability and Manufacturing LIVE.
Investing in the people
Alexander asks the people in the room to
recognise those team
members – and themselves – who are persevering despite volatility. They may not be successful, but the knowledge that they are trying their best is key.
In discussing resilience versus robustness, Alexander explains that he is a cancer survivor. When he was told he was cancer free, his plan of action for the rest of his life was not to become resilient in case the cancer came back, searching for contingency plans, but to build himself up as best as he could to mitigate the impact if it did.
"Let's invest in robustness," he says. "This is important and this is what I want to spark. Don't expect your people to be resilient all the time. You need to help them to develop robustness."
In an organisation, Alexander warns, fighting to continuously remain resilient can lead to burnout. Teams should not be fighting to stay ahead, but developing long-standing strategies where they do not need to be constantly looking over their shoulder for the next disruptor.
At Siemens, every individual has an opportunity for growth, with an aim of harvesting individual strengths throughout the organisation. Each person can have 40 hours every business year to
receive training
, whether virtual or onsite.
"We encourage everyone to be the best they can be every single day," Alexander states. "Because this is the gold, our people. It's clear for me, and I hope you have the same understanding that without people, there's no operations."

title: Tesla's new 'Accordion' Supercharger could speed up its slow buildout
content:
Tesla Supercharger
Fred Lambert
| Sep 16 2026 - 7:56 am PT
Tesla deployed its first “Accordion” Supercharger, a pre-assembled charging unit that ships 16 stalls on a single truck and installs 20% cheaper than a conventional site.
Tesla’s charging team says the goal is now to pre-assemble every Supercharger in a factory. It’s a smart move, and one the company badly needs after two years of slower deployment.
What the Accordion Supercharger is
The unit folds up like an accordion (hence the name), so one truck carries 16 V4 stalls at once. Tesla says it installs 20% cheaper than a conventional station, commissions instantly with no technician needed to energize it, and is built for sites where you can’t trench a cabinet behind a curb. It drops in between parking spaces instead.
Our first Accordion Supercharger
Our goal is to pre-assemble all Superchargers in a factory. If we can't install Superchargers behind a curb, we now have a pre-assembled solution for Superchargers between parking spaces.
16 stalls per truck shipment, 20% cheaper to install,…
“Our goal is to pre-assemble all Superchargers in a factory,” Tesla’s charging account wrote. “If we can’t install Superchargers behind a curb, we now have a pre-assembled solution for Superchargers between parking spaces.”
Behind-the-curb installs need civil work: trenching, conduit, permitting. A pre-wired island that sits between parking spaces skips most of it, which opens up tight urban and retail lots Tesla couldn’t easily build before.
Tesla has been chasing this for years
This isn’t Tesla’s first prefab rodeo. Back in
March 2022, Tesla built a full Supercharger station in just 8 days
using an early pre-fabricated system. By
April 2024, it had that down to 4 days
Then Elon Musk fired the entire Supercharger team.
late April 2024, Musk laid off all ~500 people on the charging team
, Tinucci included, in one of the most baffling calls of his tenure. Tesla rehired some of them within weeks and Musk pledged $500 million for Superchargers that year. But the damage showed up in the numbers.
The deployment still hasn’t recovered
In Q2 2024, the quarter right after the firing, Tesla added just 2,017 new Supercharger connectors worldwide. That was its slowest pace in three years, down from 2,687 the quarter before.
The buildout has been choppy ever since. Tesla added only 1,821 stalls in Q1 2025, bounced back to 3,865 in Q4 2025, then slowed again to 2,236 and 2,439 in the first two quarters of 2026.
Zoom out and the deceleration is clear. Tesla’s connector count grew 35-45% year-over-year in 2020 and 2021. As of Q2 2026, with 82,357 connectors across 8,704 stations, annual growth is down to about 17%. The network is still expanding, just nowhere near as fast as it used to, or as fast as it needs to.
Tesla’s EV deliveries stopped growing in 2024, which mitigated the slower charging infrastructure buildout, but Tesla also opened up the network to non-Tesla EVs, which are growing.
Meanwhile, BYD is lapping Tesla
Here’s the part that should worry Tesla: BYD is now putting fast chargers in the ground faster than anyone.
installed 10,000 of its 1,500 kW “flash charging” stations in five months
, from a March 2026 launch to 10,000 by late August, across 325 Chinese cities. It’s targeting 20,000 by year-end. At two guns per station, that’s roughly 40,000 charging points, approaching half of Tesla’s global stall count, built in under a year.
BYD’s chargers are also more powerful. At 1.5 MW, they take the company’s Blade 2.0 battery from 10 to 70% in about five minutes. Tesla’s V4 cabinets top out at 500 kW.
The comparison isn’t perfectly apples-to-apples. BYD’s numbers are China-mainly, with some deployment now happening in Europe and other Asian countries; Tesla’s are global, and BYD’s peak-power claims depend on its own cars. But on raw pace,
BYD is now deploying more than twice the charging power per month that Tesla is
. That gap didn’t exist two years ago.
Electrek’s Take
The Accordion Supercharger is genuinely great engineering, and exactly what Tesla should be doing. Pre-assembling whole sites in a factory is how you scale charging without scaling a giant field-construction operation, which is often complicated and varies greatly per location.
Sixteen stalls a truck, 20% cheaper, instant commissioning, and it unlocks urban sites Tesla struggled to build before. If Tesla actually hits its stated goal of pre-assembling all Superchargers, its deployment rate should climb.
But let’s be honest about why Tesla needs this so badly. The Supercharger network has been the best in the world and growing more than 35% a year until Elon fired the entire team that built it in April 2024. Two-plus years later, the deployment rate still hasn’t returned to its old trajectory. Annual growth is roughly half what it was. That was an unforced error, and Tesla is still paying for it.
Now BYD is deploying more charging power every month than Tesla, at triple the peak speed, and it’s on track for 20,000 stations in China alone this year. Tesla still has the better network for now, especially outside China. But “for now” is doing a lot of work.
Can prefab like the Accordion address that?

title: Volkswagen's new electric hot hatch delivers more power than the Golf GTI [Images]
content:
Volkswagen
Peter Johnson
| Sep 16 2026 - 7:49 am PT
Volkswagen
revealed the new ID.3 GTI, a new electric hot hatch that’s more powerful than the Golf GTI. It’s VW’s most powerful GTI ever.
Meet the new Volkswagen ID.3 GTI EV hot hatch
To celebrate the GTI’s 50th anniversary, Volkswagen introduced the most powerful series-production model ever to wear the iconic badge.
Following
the ID. Polo
, the ID.3 is Volkswagen’s second EV to get the GTI treatment. It’s also Volkswagen’s first rear-wheel-drive (RWD) GTI.
With 322 horsepower (240 kW) and 402 lb-ft (545 Nm) of torque delivered to the rear axle, the electric hot hatch can sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 5.6 seconds. In comparison, the
Golf GTI Edition 50
delivers 321 horsepower (239 kW) and accelerates from 0 to 62 mph in 5.3 seconds.
Volkswagen calls it a “true GTI” with a flexible interior and the ability to be used as an everyday vehicle.
The electric hot hatch offers “GTI Dynamics,” VW said, with an adaptive DCC sports chassis, low center of gravity, direct progressive steering, Launch Control, and a new GTI mode as standard.
GTI mode is the “secret sauce,” as Volkswagen describes it, unlocking the vehicle’s full potential. All settings are set to “maximum sportiness,” including the drive, chassis, rear motor, and steering.
Meanwhile, the new Launch Control can be activated, changing the background lighting to red and switching the Digital Cockpit to GTI mode.
Like the Hyundai IONIQ 5 N, Volkswagen’s new ID.3 GTI replicates the sound of a traditional combustion engine sports car.
As expected, the electric hot hatch features plenty of GTI badges inside and out. It also features VW’s new front-end design with a red stripe in tribute to the first Golf GTI launched in 1976, plus new 20″ Wörthersee wheels.
Volkswagen ID.3 GTI and ID. Polo GTI (Source: Volkswagen)
According to Volkswagen, the new ID.3 GTI hot hatch is “one of the sportiest electric vehicles in its class.”
Inside, Volkswagen’s electric hot hatch features GTI elements throughout, including a red stripe that runs across the dashboard, a red 12 o’clock marking on the new multifunction steering wheel, and premium sports seats.
It also includes Volkswagen’s new infotainment system and Digital Cockpit with a larger 12.9″ infotainment screen and 10″ instrument cluster. VW is bringing back physical buttons, which are now found under the infotainment and on the steering wheel.
Based on the new VW ID.3 Neo, the GTI variant uses the larger 79 kWh battery, which provides up to 373 miles (601 km) of WLTP range.
With DC fast charging of up to 183 kW, the electric ID.3 GTI’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in about 29 minutes.
Volkswagen will open pre-sales for the new ID.3 GTI in early 2027. We will learn prices closer to launch, but it will likely be a bit more than
the ID. Polo GTI
, which starts at 39,000 euros ($45,000) in Germany.

title: Rivian’s ALSO e-bikes are finally hitting the road – but not for frustrated customers
content:
Micah Toll
| Sep 16 2026 - 5:33 am PT
Rivian spin-off ALSO is finally getting its futuristic TM-B electric bikes out across the United States.
Unfortunately for the customers who ordered them nearly a year ago, those bikes aren’t headed to their garages. They’re headed on tour.
ALSO has kicked off its “Test Spin Fall Tour,” a traveling demo program that will bring the high-tech TM-B to cities around the country from September through November. The tour started in Portland, Oregon, and includes stops in Philadelphia, Boston, Boise, Madison, Minneapolis, Sacramento, Atlanta, Bentonville, San Antonio, Nashville, Detroit, Salt Lake City, Dallas, Tempe,
and more
The company is bringing demo bikes along so prospective new customers can get an in-depth walkthrough and actually ride the TM-B before potentially placing an order.
While ALSO is driving TM-Bs around the country to woo new customers, many of its earliest customers are still waiting for the bikes they already paid for.
The $4,500 Launch Edition TM-B was originally expected to begin reaching customers in spring 2026. That timeline slipped into summer, then into September. Earlier this month, customers received
yet another update
saying Launch Edition bikes were “now shipping,” but that deliveries would occur in waves stretching all the way into early November.
As of last week, several early reservation holders on Reddit – including self-described day-one customers – were
still reporting
that they hadn’t received individual delivery dates.
Others have sounded the alarm about worrying signs of a stunted rollout, including
multiple reports
of customers visiting local bike shops listed on the ALSO site as service providers, only for the staff there to not even know they’re considered to be official ALSO service partners.
To ALSO’s credit, the company has recently made a more concerted effort to explain what has gone wrong.
Following growing criticism from customers over both the delays and a perceived lack of communication, ALSO Head of Product Saul Leiken
took to Reddit
with a lengthy explanation and apology.
According to Leiken, part of the problem stems from supply-chain issues affecting the raw materials used for printed circuit boards and certain integrated circuits. ALSO says demand associated with the AI boom has made some components difficult to source, in some cases forcing engineers to source and requalify alternative materials – which means more engineering and testing instead of simply swapping in another part.
There’s also the battery.
The TM-B’s removable battery is particularly unusual because it supports USB-C Power Delivery charging at up to 240W. According to ALSO’s explanation, that level of power exceeds existing regulatory guidelines for the application, requiring the company to work with standards organizations on new safety and testing protocols. The bike’s unusual DreamRide pedal-by-wire drivetrain has created another manufacturing challenge, requiring what Leiken described as high-precision production and a slower ramp to maintain quality.
Leiken acknowledged that the company should have communicated those challenges more clearly along the way.
That explanation certainly provides more context for why one of the most technologically ambitious e-bikes we’ve seen in years has proven difficult to manufacture at scale, though the company’s discussion of some of those efforts in the present tense does raise questions about the veracity of the “now shipping” claims made by ALSO earlier this month.
In all fairness, building what amounts to a software-defined light electric vehicle with a novel drivetrain and battery architecture was probably never going to be as straightforward as ordering a few hub motors and welding together some aluminum frames.
But it also creates an increasingly strange situation for ALSO’s earliest supporters.
There are apparently enough functional TM-Bs available to send fleets of them around the country so prospective buyers can take test rides. ALSO has also been operating Test Spin programs through Rivian locations, part of an effort announced earlier this year to bring demo rides to ten cities nationwide.
Meanwhile, some of the people who put down $4,500 for their e-bikes last year are still checking their inboxes for an actual delivery date.
Obviously, demo and production bikes aren’t necessarily interchangeable. Marketing fleets are allocated long in advance, and pulling a handful of demo bikes off a nationwide tour wouldn’t magically solve a production ramp involving hundreds or thousands of customer units.
But optics matter here, too.
Seeing an ALSO van roll into your city full of shiny TM-Bs has to feel a little different when you ordered yours last October and are still waiting for the email telling you when yours will arrive.
The good news is that ALSO still maintains that Launch Edition production is underway and that deliveries are coming in waves through early November.
Hopefully, the next nationwide tour these bikes embark on will be inside delivery trucks headed to the customers who have been waiting for them.
View this post on Instagram
Electrek’s Take
Look, from a marketing standpoint, a tour like this makes plenty of sense. The TM-B is an impressive engineering feat, but also a pretty weird bike – in the best possible way. It probably benefits more than most from getting butts in seats. Its unconventional frame, removable top tube/seat assembly, touchscreen interface, high-powered USB-C charging, and pedal-by-wire DreamRide drivetrain make it unlike basically anything else in the e-bike industry.
These are all things you have to feel to understand. And I imagine that they feel pretty impressive, though I can’t necessarily speak from personal experience. Readers may recall that I wrote an exclusive last year ahead of ALSO’s highly anticipated and secretive launch, revealing that the company had accidentally leaked their own bike’s design from a few poorly-edited frames in a flashy teaser video. An hour later, I received an email uninviting me from the ALSO launch. So while I can appreciate the impressive engineering that went into the bike, I can’t tell you how the bike rides – at least not unless the tour stops in my city.
But from a distance, I can appreciate the dueling desires here, for a new company to get its bikes out there as broadly as possible for the public to see and ride, and to meanwhile calm frustrated customers who have no idea when they’ll get their own paid-in-full e-bikes after months of delays.
There’s no doubt that ALSO has the engineering talent to pull this off. The question is whether the other pieces of running a successful e-bike company will fall into place.

title: Poland's solar pipeline hits 40.6 GW - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
An independent Polish research institute says its latest database of solar projects with grid-connection conditions has grown to 40.6 GW, even as the number of tracked projects fell under a revised methodology that excludes inactive projects.
Brian Publicover
16 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Katowice, Poland
Instytut Energetyki Odnawialnej (IEO), a Warsaw-based research group founded in 2001, said its August 2026 database identified 6,450 solar projects holding grid-connection conditions in Poland, with a combined capacity of 40.6 GW, alongside 5,212 projects that have secured building permits.
The figures come from IEO’s database of PV projects in Poland, published periodically since 2018 and compiled from public connection data released by the country’s four main distribution system operators – Enea Operator, Energa-Operator, PGE Dystrybucja and Tauron Dystrybucja – along with PSE, the transmission system operator.
The August figures are not directly comparable with IEO’s previous edition, published in December 2025, which counted 7,703 projects with valid connection conditions totaling 33.4 GW. IEO said it applied a stricter methodology in the latest edition, filtering out projects it judged inactive or “dead” based on operator data, including connection conditions older than two years and connection agreements older than four years that had not progressed further.
That change means the drop in project count, from 7,703 to 6,450, should not be read as a sign of market contraction. Aggregate pipeline capacity rose by more than 7 GW over the same period, consistent with trends in IEO’s earlier database editions, which showed fewer projects obtaining connection conditions while associated capacity increased. In the first three quarters of 2025, IEO recorded 936 new projects gaining connection conditions, down from 1,271 in the same period of 2024, even as the associated capacity increased.
IEO said the accumulated pipeline could be drawn on if renewable-energy auctions are announced in 2026 and later in 2027, although no official timetable had been published by Poland’s Energy Regulatory Office (URE) at the time of writing. IEO said the scale of the pipeline suggests the potential for stronger competition for auction volumes, which could affect auction prices.

title: Norway hits 1 GW solar milestone - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Multiconsult’s Hassan Gholami tells
pv magazine
that with Norway’s achievement coinciding with a market slowdown, the country needs to develop its large-scale market and encourage solar energy sharing to ramp up annual deployments.
Patrick Jowett
16 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
Utility-scale
Norway’s installed solar capacity has surpassed 1 GW, standing at 1,003 MW as of mid-September, according to Elhub, the country’s central database where Norwegian grid companies register all electricity meters and report metered data.
The milestone builds on the
that were counted by the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate’s (NVE) solar dashboard as of the end of July.
Hassan Gholami, a senior consultant on solar and storage at Multiconsult, told
pv magazine
that the difference in the two databases is down to processing times, with Elhub updating daily and NVE’s updating monthly and occasionally adding installation figures retrospectively from previous months.
“If 2026 ends within the 80 to 100 MW [of annual additions] I expect, NVE’s dashboard will also pass 1 GW around the end of the year,” he said. “My advice to market participants is to use NVE as the official reference and Elhub as the earliest signal of what is happening.”
Gholami said passing the 1 GW threshold highlights that “solar is now a permanent part of the Norwegian power system, even if it is still a small one.” He added that solar makes a natural partner to Norway’s hydropower, which supplies around 90% of the country’s electricity
“Dry years, when low rainfall leaves reservoirs short of water, tend to be sunnier and therefore good years for solar production. In wet years, solar tends to produce less, but reservoirs are full and hydropower has plenty of water to work with,” Gholami explained. “As solar grows, it will help Norway make even better use of its reservoirs as seasonal storage, making the power system less vulnerable to dry years and more secure overall.”
In reaching 1 GW of solar, Norway follows in the footsteps of its Scandinavian neighbours Denmark, which reached 1 GW around 2018 and Sweden, which hit the milestone in 2020.
But while Denmark and Sweden have enjoyed record years for solar deployment since, Norway’s annual installations are currently slowing, with this year predicted to be the lowest annual figure since 2021. Its record for solar deployment in a calendar year dates back to 2023, at around around 300 MW.
Gholami said that in order to begin developing larger annual volumes, Norway should look to develop a steady flow of larger scale solar parks, similar to Denmark, or a mass rooftop market, as seen in Sweden.
He also emphasised that building larger-scale solar parks will be integral if Norway wants to move towards deploying 1 GW a year.
Norway’s larger-scale market is still in its infancy, with reports from NVE revealing that, as of May this year, only five of 16 licensed solar parks in Norway had been built, which Gholami said points to weak profitability and lack of grid capacity.
“A single 20 MW to 30 MW park equals roughly a fifth to a third of all the solar Norway is expected to install this year, so two or three parks completed in 2027 and 2028 would change the annual figures noticeably. But that is still far below the several hundred megawatts per year Denmark’s large parks have delivered,” he explained.
“For Norway to get near 1 GW per year, licensing and municipal approvals need to deliver 300 MW to 500 MW of new parks every year, and those parks must actually be built. This is the most important condition, and there is no sign yet that it will be met.”
Gholami added that rules allowing people to share solar power would help Norway develop a mature rooftop market, similar to Sweden.
Norway’s residential market currently lies at an almost-standstill, in part down to an optional fixed electricity price for households known as the Norgepris that has removed most of the financial incentive for rooftop solar.
However, the Norwegian Parliament has ordered a study on a guaranteed minimum price for building-mounted solar power exported to the grid, due this year. “It is the first serious movement on the demand side in several years, and its outcome will largely decide whether homeowners return to the market,” Gholami explained.
Gholami concluded that if solar large parks are licensed and built faster, and rules for sharing solar power are expanded further, annual installations could rise noticeably from 2027 and 2028 as the first licensed parks are completed. Under this trajectory, he suggested Norway could plausibly reach 1 GW per year around 2030 or 2031.
“However, if licensing stalls and the market relies on rooftops alone, annual installations will likely stay between 100 MW and 300 MW for the rest of the decade, and the second gigawatt will take almost as long as the first,” he told
pv magazine

title: Guinea plans solar, storage procurement program - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Belgian non-profit organisation RELP is working with the West African nation to design and structure a competitive procurement program for solar PV and battery storage projects.
Patrick Jowett
16 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Guinea’s Ministry of Energy and Belgium-headquartered clean energy non-profit RELP have signed an agreement to cooperate on a competitive procurement program for solar PV and battery energy storage projects.
Under the terms of the agreement, the two parties will work on the design, sizing and structuring of the program, with RELP tasked with providing technical, legal, regulatory and financial advisory support to the Ministry, working alongside the country’s National Directorate for Renewable Energy as technical counterpart.
The procurement program is expected to kick off with a first indicative phase covering 400 MW.
A statement published by RELP says its support will include the drafting of full tender documentation, helping with capacity building and supporting the ministry in the adoption of risk mitigation and credit enhancement instruments
“Clean, reliable, affordable electricity is the foundation of Guinea’s ambitions. But how it is procured matters just as much: transparent rules and a credible plan are what turn a single programme into a lasting market,” commented Aminata Bocar Ba, RELP’s Africa Engagement Manager. “That is the partnership we want to build.”
The Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) has identified 329.7 MW of operational solar in Guinea to date, according to figures in its online project database, the majority of which is unidentified C&I projects.
RELP is also working with West African nations Ghana, Togo and Senegal on similar government-led renewable energy procurements, according to a social media post from the company.
Its agreement with Ghana, entered into last month, includes designing and implementing a multi-year competitive procurement program for renewable energy and battery energy storage, including the country’s first public renewables auction.

title: BYD launches 62 MWh GC Block for gigawatt-scale battery storage plants - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
BYD Energy Storage has launched a standardized battery storage unit with three configurations covering two- to six-hour applications and up to 62 MWh of capacity.
Vincent Shaw
16 Sep 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
BYD Energy Storage has launched GC Block, a standardized station-level battery storage unit with configurations of up to 62 MWh, as part of its second-generation GW-scale grid-forming energy storage solution.
The company unveiled the product this week at the 2026 Energy Green Development Conference and International Digital Energy Expo in Shenzhen. It positioned GC Block as the core building block of its gigawatt-scale grid-forming energy storage solution 2.0, alongside the new GC Flux PCS 2.0 power conversion system and GC Master EMS 2.0 energy management system.
GC Block is available in three standardized configurations: 7.5 MW/15.5 MWh for roughly two-hour applications, 7.5 MW/31 MWh for four-hour projects, and 10 MW/62 MWh for six-hour storage. At the largest configuration, a 1 GWh project would require about 17 GC Blocks, according to BYD.
The system uses BYD’s 1,980 Ah energy storage Blade Battery cells manufactured using a stacking process. BYD said the architecture reduces the number of cells required in a large-scale project while simplifying cabling, foundations, battery management and maintenance. For a GW-scale plant, the company claims the design can cut battery management complexity by 69.4%, maintenance workload by more than 60%, and installation and commissioning work by more than 18%.
The company is positioning GC Block as a move beyond individual containerized storage units toward larger, repeatable power station modules. The standardized architecture is intended for utility-scale standalone storage, renewable-plus-storage projects, data center power applications, zero-carbon industrial parks, and storage supporting high-power EV charging infrastructure.
BYD also introduced GC Flux PCS 2.0, covering power ratings from 1.25 MW to 15.6 MW. A standard 20-foot PCS container can accommodate up to 10 MW, with maximum conversion efficiency of 99.5% and three-times overload capability for 10 seconds. The system supports both centralized and string-based storage architectures.
The accompanying GC Master EMS 2.0 is designed for online management of GW-scale storage fleets. BYD said the platform incorporates AI-based forecasting with 98.5% prediction accuracy and can automatically calculate and dispatch storage resources without continuous manual supervision.
One distinction is important when interpreting the headline 62 MWh figure. It does not refer to the energy capacity of a single 20-foot battery container. GC Block is what BYD calls a “station-level standard unit,” comprising a larger integrated section of a storage plant. The 62 MWh figure represents the total capacity of the largest 10 MW/62 MWh configuration. BYD has not yet publicly disclosed the exact number of battery containers, overall dimensions, or physical layout within that block.
BYD describes the 62 MWh configuration as the highest-capacity station-level standardized storage unit it has launched. The product reflects the increasing scale of utility storage projects, with system suppliers seeking to reduce engineering complexity by shifting more integration work from individual site construction toward standardized, repeatable plant modules.

, with analysis suggesting the country is on track to surpass 1 GW of installed solar by the end of the year.

title: Overcapacity in modules, underdeveloped upstream: The next challenge for Indian PV manufacturing - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Solar cell manufacturing is significantly more capital-intensive and technologically more challenging than module manufacturing, with manufacturers remaining reliant on imported equipment. Consequently, ongoing geopolitical uncertainties affecting equipment sourcing, coupled with plant stabilisation challenges following commissioning, could delay cell capacity additions across industry players.
Rachit Mehta, Vice President & Sector Head, ICRA
16 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Renewable energy (RE) plus large hydro-based power generation capacity increased at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of ~12% since March 2014 and stood at 296 GW as of August 2026, constituting ~53% of the overall power generating capacity, led by strong policy support and improving tariff competitiveness. The solar power segment remained the key driver of capacity addition in the RE sector, with installed capacity increasing from less than 3 GW in March 2014 to 168 GW in August 2026.
In anticipation of healthy growth prospects, India’s solar photovoltaic (PV) module manufacturing capacity increased significantly from less than 20 GW in 2022 to 217 GW as of August 2026. This expansion was supported by favourable policy measures, specifically the approved list of models and manufacturers (ALMM), which effectively restricted the direct import of solar modules.
However, the operational module manufacturing capacity is lower than installed capacity, given that some module facilities continue to be constrained by older technologies (Polycrystalline and MonoPERC) and lower-wattage modules that no longer align with current market demand which is tilted towards TOPCon and Heterojunction modules.
Nevertheless, even after factoring in the lower operational capacity, the annual solar module production is expected to be higher than the projected annual solar capacity installation of 55-60 gigawatt direct current (GWdc). Further, uncertainty surrounding U.S. tariff measures has led to a diversion of modules from export markets to the domestic market, exacerbating supply pressures. Hence, the overcapacity in module production will likely accelerate consolidation in the module manufacturing industry, directly impacting the smaller, pure-play module players.
Just as the ALMM support led to capacity addition in the module manufacturing space, the extension of ALMM requirements to solar photovoltaic (PV) cells from June 2026 has accelerated investments in cell capacity addition. Consequently, cell manufacturing capacity has increased from 13 GW in July 2025 to 35 GW as of August 2026 and is likely to increase to 100 GW by December 2027.
However, cell manufacturing is more capital intensive, with investment requirement of INR 400-500 crore per GW compared to INR 80-90 crore per GW for module manufacturing. Further, cell manufacturing remains considerably more challenging than module manufacturing from a technology perspective, with reliance on imported equipment.
Consequently, ongoing geopolitical uncertainties affecting equipment sourcing, coupled with plant stabilisation issues post commissioning, could delay cell capacity addition across players.
Further upstream in the solar manufacturing value chain are ingot, wafer and polysilicon manufacturing, which are more technologically complex than module and cell manufacturing. ALMM list for solar wafers, which requires manufacturers to have equivalent ingot manufacturing capacity, is proposed to become effective from June 2028. However, this list will not be issued unless there are at least three wafer manufacturing units with aggregate capacity of 15 GW per annum.
While one player has completed an ingot and wafer facility (2 GW), the overall progress towards wafer and polysilicon capacity addition remains slow despite plans announced by the big players. Further, in absence of policy support such as ALMM, the domestic manufactured components are unlikely to be competitive vis-à-vis Chinese imports. This reflects the technological complexity of ingot and wafer manufacturing, along with challenges related to process know-how and technology transfer. Other factors hindering growth in the polysilicon and wafer segment include the high capital and operational costs of setting up the plant.
Hence, the pace of domestic ingot/wafer capacity addition remains to be seen. Nevertheless, the vertically integrated manufacturers are expected to benefit in the long term due to greater control over the supply chain.
Margin pressure for module players; cell margins may moderate as capacity expands
Based on prevailing imported cell prices and considering the operating costs for domestic original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), the landed cost of modules from domestic OEMs using imported solar PV cells comes at 13-15 cents/watt. However, given the significant capacity addition in module manufacturing, these prices have come under pressure, thereby impacting the profitability for standalone module manufacturers.
Further, the cost of manufacturing solar PV cells in India is higher than the cost of imported PV cells and thus, the cost of modules manufactured using domestic cells comes at 21-23 cents/watt. With these changes, the capex cost for solar plant is likely to increase by around 15-17%, thereby leading to increase in solar tariffs going forward.
While domestic cell manufacturers currently benefit from limited domestic capacity, resulting in relatively higher margins than standalone module manufacturers and higher module prices for modules manufactured using domestic cells, both margins and prices are expected to moderate over the medium term as additional cell manufacturing capacity is commissioned and manufacturers achieve scale efficiencies in cell production. However, the implementation of ALMM requirements for wafers from June 2028 could partially offset the expected moderation by increasing module prices, while also resulting in higher project costs and, consequently, exerting upward pressure on solar power tariffs.

title: Symmetry-breaking molecular strategy pushes inverted perovskite solar cell efficiency to 26.32% - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers used symmetry-breaking co-assembly to improve SAM coverage and interface quality in inverted perovskite solar cells, achieving a 26.32% efficiency and a certified result of 25.67%. An encapsulated device retained 93% of its initial efficiency after 1,150 hours of maximum power point operation.
Lior Kahana
16 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
The devices
An international research group has developed a novel strategy to improve self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) used as hole-transport layers in inverted perovskite solar cells. The method, called symmetry-breaking co-assembly (SBC), combines symmetric and asymmetric molecules to suppress aggregation and improve surface coverage.
“Rather than synthesizing complex and costly asymmetric molecules, we achieve the benefits of molecular asymmetry by co-assembling a widely used symmetric SAM (MeO-2PACz) with a simple asymmetric conjugated molecule (DTCA),” corresponding author Tom Wu told
pv magazine
. “This approach suppresses molecular self-aggregation, substantially increases surface coverage, and improves buried-interface quality.”
Wu said his team also developed a quantitative atomic force microscopy-infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR) method to directly measure SAM coverage at the nanoscale.
“Together, these advances enabled certified efficiencies above 25.6% and excellent operational stability, providing a practical new framework for interface engineering in perovskite photovoltaics,” he added.
The researchers selected MeO-2PACz as the host molecule and compared it with two symmetry-breaking co-assemblies incorporating either 2-thiophenecarboxylic acid (TCA) or dibenzo[b,d]thiophene-4-carboxylic acid (DTCA). They deposited the MeO-2PACz, MeO-TCA and MeO-DTCA formulations from 0.7 mg/mL isopropanol solutions onto plasma-treated indium tin oxide (ITO) substrates by spin coating at 3,000 rpm for 30 seconds. They then annealed the samples at 100 C for 10 minutes.
Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that DTCA rapidly anchored to the ITO substrate and suppressed MeO-2PACz aggregation. AFM-IR measurements showed surface coverage of 60.6% for MeO-2PACz alone, 62.2% for MeO-TCA and 82.4% for MeO-DTCA.
The team also compared MeO-DTCA molar ratios of 3:1, 4:1 and 5:1 and tested DTCA alone. It identified the 4:1 mixture as the optimal formulation.
The molecular assembly | Image: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
“By mixing the industry-standard symmetric SAM MeO-2PACz with a small asymmetric molecule (DTCA), we increased SAM surface coverage by more than 30%, as directly quantified using a newly developed AFM-IR analysis method,” Wu said. “We were amazed to find that strategically breaking molecular symmetry could unlock so many benefits for solar cells, leading to improvements in interface quality, energy conversion efficiency, and operational stability.”
The scientists built the cell with an inverted configuration. It was based on an indium tin oxide (ITO) substrate, a MeO-DTCA co-assembled SAM as the hole-selective layer (HTL), a perovskite absorber, a phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM) electron-transport layer (ETL), a bathocuproine (BCP) buffer layer and a silver (Ag) electrode.
They explained that, when the surface coverage of co-SAM layers is maximized, the interfacial chemical reaction under electrical stress and the non-radiative recombination loss were effectively suppressed, resulting in power conversion efficiencies of 26.32% and 25.34% for areas of 0.08 cm2 and 1 cm2, respectively. The encapsulated device retained 93% of its initial efficiency after operating at the maximum power point (MPP) for 1,150 hours.
“This study opens several exciting directions for future research,” concluded Wu. “The novel strategy is likely applicable to many other molecular systems, and we are interested in developing a broader library of symmetry-breaking molecular combinations and establishing design rules that link molecular symmetry, dipole moment, and surface coverage. Second, we aim to translate these molecular design principles to large-area modules and tandem solar cells. Finally, our quantitative AFM-IR methodology provides a new way to study ultrathin molecular layers in a quantitative approach, which could benefit not only photovoltaics but also other devices involving such molecular layers.”
The research, “
Symmetry-Breaking Co-Assembly of Conjugated Molecules Boosts Perovskite Photovoltaics
,” was published in Nature Communications. Scientists from China’s
Hong Kong Polytechnic University
Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology
Chinese Academy of Sciences
Northwestern Polytechnical University
, and Great Bay University, Australia’s
University of New South Wales
, the United Kingdom’s
University of Surrey
, South Korea’s
Korea University
, and Germany’s
Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT)
participated in the study.

title: Hithium launches 4 MWh sodium-ion BESS with new 785Ah cell - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Hithium unveiled the ∞Power N4.0MWh, a 4 MWh sodium-ion storage system featuring a 785 Ah cell, 20,000-cycle life, and 30-year design life. Full-scale production is planned for 2027, initially targeting utilities before expanding to commercial, industrial, and residential markets.
Tristan Rayner
16 Sep 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Chinese battery maker Hithium held a product launch for its next sodium-ion energy storage solution, announcing the ∞Power N4.0MWh, a 4 MWh sodium-ion energy storage system equipped with the new high-capacity ∞Cell N785Ah sodium-ion battery, representing a huge step up in capacity that’s been achieved in less than two years.
In the launch, Hithium also announced that while its timeline is starting with utility-scale storage, it will expand from utility-scale storage into commercial and industrial and residential products, bringing more battery chemistry options to businesses and households.
Hithium said it plans to begin full-scale production and delivery in 2027 using its existing lithium-ion manufacturing lines, and will offer a 30-year designed service life. Its aim is to rapidly move
sodium-ion technology
∞Cell N785Ah
wikimedia commons
The ∞Cell N785Ah cell features a 20,000-cycle service life, supports 2- to 8- hour storage durations, and is “fully compatible” with Hithium’s 1,000 Ah lithium-ion manufacturing platform, including cell and system integration production lines, supporting the production scale-up.
“Energy storage technologies must overcome two barriers to achieve large-scale deployment: affordability and availability,” said Nazar Yi, chief technology officer for Hithium.
Hithium had previously launched the ∞Cell N162 Ah in December 2024, which it called the first sodium-ion battery specifically designed for utility-scale energy storage, and less than two years later, has stepped its cell structure to larger-format 785 Ah cells.
New 4 MWh sodium-based ESS
The ∞Power N4.0MWh’s sodium-ion architecture features a stacked-cell design which has reduced the station footprint by 30%, a dedicated BMS with SOC estimation accuracy of ≤2.5%, and compatibility with 800–1500V PCS. Compared with Hithium’s first generation sodium-ion ESS, the PCS rated-power utilization is more than 20% higher.
Hithium said a new thermal management approach was via a hybrid air-liquid cooling pairing, with what it described as a “24-hour comprehensive efficiency of over 88%”. Thermal management is further boosted with weather data being used to decide on the style of cooling, which can reduce auxiliary power consumption by 30% and standby auxiliary power consumption by 50%.
“30 years means 10,950 days of validation, a long-term commitment to our customers,” said Aileen Wang, director of Battery Research Institute.
Hithium also said it is targeting a quoted levelized cost of storage of a RMB 0.1 per kWh, or USD ~1.5 cents per kWh.
Livestream
The official launch event takes place at 4PM in China, or 10 AM CEST / 4 AM ET with a
stream on YouTube

title: Parapet walls reshape airflow, soiling patterns in rooftop PV systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
UK researchers found that rooftop parapets reshape airflow and PV dust deposition, with effects varying by wind speed, particle size, panel tilt, and array position. Their wind-tunnel study shows that parapet height alone cannot predict soiling, highlighting the need for site-specific PV design and maintenance strategies.
Emiliano Bellini
16 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Commercial & industrial
Residential
The experimental setup
Researchers at the
University of Nottingham
in the United Kingdom have investigated how parapet height affects dust accumulation on rooftop PV systems. They found that parapet walls substantially alter rooftop airflow, but their effect on particle deposition depends on wind speed and particle size.
“As rooftop solar expands worldwide, soiling is becoming an increasingly important operational issue,” corresponding author Yupeng Wu told
pv magazine
. “Our work highlights that the building itself can influence that problem. Even a relatively simple feature such as a parapet wall can change the airflow and, therefore, how airborne particles interact with the PV array.
“We found that this effect is not straightforward. A higher parapet does not necessarily lead to more or less particle deposition, because the outcome depends on wind speed and particle size. We also found that the most exposed part of the PV array can shift from the front rows to panels farther downstream under different conditions,” he went on to say.
The researchers combined physical modeling, computational fluid dynamics-discrete phase modeling (CFD-DPM), experimental validation, and mechanistic analysis. Their idealized, full-scale configuration featured an 18-meter-by-18-meter flat-roof building with a height of 10 meters and five PV rows facing the incoming wind.
They modeled parapet heights of 0 meters, 0.5 meters, and 1.5 meters to represent unshielded, partially shielded, and fully shielded configurations, respectively. Atmospheric inlet velocities of 1.3 m/s, 2.6 m/s, and 3.9 m/s represented different wind conditions.
The DPM tracked particle transport and deposition, while a discrete random-walk model represented unresolved turbulent dispersion, particularly for small, low-inertia particles. The researchers validated the airflow model through wind-tunnel tests using an approximately 1:60-scale model. They then used the CFD-DPM framework to assess the effects of parapet height, wind speed, particle size, and PV tilt angle.
Airflow in rooftop PV systems surrounded by parapet walls
The researchers conducted experiments in a 3.1-meter-by-2.4-meter-by-1.8-meter atmospheric boundary-layer wind tunnel with an 11.5-meter fetch. Sixty pressure taps installed across five PV modules provided additional validation of the CFD-predicted rooftop pressure field. The study considered only normal wind incidence, so the findings do not account for asymmetric airflow and deposition under oblique winds.
The analysis showed that taller parapets suppress rooftop airflow and enlarge low-velocity recirculation zones around PV modules. However, despite reducing near-surface turbulence, tall parapets may shield the panels by directing particles above the array.
Higher wind speeds strengthened vortices and particle transport without substantially changing the geometry-controlled flow pattern. Fine particles followed the airflow and were rarely deposited, while larger particles were increasingly influenced by inertia and gravity.
The tests also showed that windward rows dominated deposition at low wind speeds. At higher speeds, recirculation redirected entrained particles toward downstream rows. PV tilt had a non-monotonic effect, with horizontal panels collecting the most dust and panels tilted at 60 degrees deflecting more particles over the array.
Overall, particle deposition reflected the combined effects of particle delivery, shielding, recirculation, ventilation, settling, and inertia.
“The parapet displaces the roof-edge shear layer and changes particle access to the PV array,” the researchers said. “A shallow parapet can create a partly enclosed recirculation region that promotes local interception for selected particle sizes and wind conditions. A taller parapet can increase shielding and allow more particles to be transported over the array.
“The response reflects competition among recirculation, near-roof ventilation, turbulent transport, inertial impaction, gravitational settling, and penetration between rows. Parapet height therefore does not produce a universally increasing or decreasing deposition rate.”
Particle size was the main factor governing deposition. Fine particles followed the airflow and were rarely captured, while the peak deposition diameter shifted from 100 μm at 1.3 m/s to between 150 μm and 200 μm at 2.6 m/s, and between 200 μm and 300 μm at 3.9 m/s. Coarser particles were deposited mainly on windward rows.
The researchers concluded that parapet height alone cannot reliably predict rooftop PV soiling. They said system design and maintenance planning should account for local wind conditions, airborne particle sizes, panel tilt, and array position, as these factors jointly determine where and how strongly dust is deposited.
Their findings are presented in “
Effects of rooftop parapet walls on airflow and dust deposition on photovoltaic arrays: A CFD–DPM study
,” published in
Building and Environment
